newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN considers compromise on rights expert for Congo.
newsitem.headline: UN considers compromise on rights expert for Congo.

text.p: The United Nations, at the insistence of officials from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, may drop its chief human rights investigator probing the alleged killings of Rwandan refugees, diplomats said.

The compromise, supported by the United States, is to enable a long-delayed U.N. investigation into the refugee crisis to go ahead now that President Laurent Kabila has given the green light, the envoys said.

Roberto Garreton, a Chilean lawyer and special U.N. human rights investigator, headed a U.N. commission of inquiry in April to probe allegations of masacres of Rwanda Hutu refugees but the group was refused entry by Kabila.

At the time, Kabila's aides insisted Garreton be dropped from the group, that the mission include local officials and army officers and that the background of forensic experts from Argentina be vetted.

An expert on the Congo, Garreton has produced a 16-page report that includs a list of 40 sites of killings allegedly committed by soldiers loyal to Kabila in the eastern part of the country, then known as Zaire.
Kabila, first in talks with Secretary-General Kofi Annan and then with American U.N. ambassador Bill Richardson, agreed to an advance team arriving on June 20 so that the probe could begin on July 7.

Kabila's takeover last month of Africa's third largest country after a seven-month bush war, has been tainted by reports that his troops have systematically killed Hutu refugees. Among them are militias implicated in the 1994 genocide against Rwandan Tutsis and Hutus.

Annan at a news conference on Thursday did not mention Garreton but he said the acting U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, Ralph Zacklin, would meet him on Friday to plan the mission. The controversy over Garreton would be discussed then, according to the diplomats.

Kabila, according to Annan, "has begun to realise the importance and urgency of resolving, and the need to resolve these issues -- not only the humanitarian issue but also the question of human rights and the investigation into the alleged mass murders."
He said that at the end of their recent disucssions the Zimbabwean capital of Harare, Kabila told him: "I also want to get this albatross off my neck."
